subtitle: Describe a database table as a Python class, and let Django build it for you.
notes: This deck goes with exercise 3. By the end you should be able to write a model with fields, defaults, a default ordering and your own methods.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
A backend must **remember** things between requests, so it keeps them in a **database**. A database table looks like a DataFrame: named **columns**, one **row** per record.

The difference: a table is **strict**. You decide up front each column's name, type and rules. In Django you write that plan as a Python class, a **model**, and Django builds the table.
slides.notes: Picture the books table: columns id, title, author, published_year, is_available. Each row comes back to you as a Python object, so book.title is that one book's title.

slides.title: What the tests do with your class
slides.caption: There's no function to call: the tests use your `Book` class directly.
slides.code:
Book._meta.get_field("author").max_length     # expects 100

book = Book.objects.create(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert")
book.is_available     # expects True (nobody set it)
book.created_at       # expects a date and time, not None
str(book)             # expects "Dune by Frank Herbert"

# saved as Neuromancer, Dune, Foundation; expected back in this order:
# ["Dune", "Foundation", "Neuromancer"]

Book(title="1984", author="Orwell", published_year=1949).is_classic()  # True
Book(title="X", author="Y", published_year=1950).is_classic()          # False
Book(title="Unknown", author="Anon").is_classic()                      # False
slides.notes: Before the tests run, the grader builds the table from your model. _meta.get_field is how the tests inspect a field; you won't need _meta in your own code. 1950 is not before 1950, so it's not a classic.

slides.title: New words

terms.meaning: A Python class that describes one table.
One attribute of a model. It becomes one column.
One row, as a Python value: `Book(title="Dune")`.
"No value": the database says `NULL`, Python says `None`.
A function inside a class; `self` is the one object it's called on.
A file that updates the database tables to match your models.

slides.notes: The ORM is the part of Django that turns Python like Book.objects.create(...) into database commands, so you never write SQL yourself.

slides.title: Tools: field types
slides.caption: Each field is one line inside the class. The options set the rules for that column.
slides.code:
class Movie(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=150)                       # text
    runtime = models.PositiveIntegerField(null=True, blank=True)  # optional
    is_showing = models.BooleanField(default=False)               # yes / no
    added_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)            # automatic
slides.notes: CharField always needs max_length. default= is used when nobody gives a value. auto_now_add=True sets the date and time once, when the row is first saved; you never set it yourself.

slides.title: null=True vs blank=True

left.heading: null=True
bullets: Without it, saving no value fails

right.heading: blank=True
bullets: Forms and serializers allow it empty
The user may leave it out

slides.notes: Every field is required unless you say otherwise. An optional number needs both options: the database must accept no value, and input checks must allow an empty one.

slides.title: Tool: making and saving objects
slides.caption: `Book(...)` lives in memory only. `.save()` writes it; `objects.create(...)` does both.
slides.code:
book = Book(title="Emma")
print(book.title)            # Emma
print(book.pk)               # None  (not saved yet)
book.save()
print(book.pk)               # 1  (the database gave it an id)
Book.objects.create(title="Beloved")
print(Book.objects.count())  # 2
slides.notes: pk means primary key: the row's id. The Console starts with an empty database each time you run something.

slides.title: Tool: class Meta and ordering
slides.caption: Settings for the whole table go in a small class inside the model.
slides.notes: ordering is a list, so it needs square brackets. The - in front reverses the order. Without it, rows come back in whatever order the database likes, usually the order they were saved.

slides.title: Tool: methods and __str__
slides.caption: A plain Python class (not a model) with both kinds of method:
slides.notes: Python calls __str__ for print(obj) or str(obj), and it must return a string. You call your own methods with brackets, film.is_old(), but never pass self yourself.

slides.title: Pattern: check for None first
slides.caption: `None < 1950` crashes with a `TypeError`. `and` stops early, so check for `None` first.
slides.code:
score = None
print(score is not None and score > 50)

score = 72
print(score is not None and score > 50)
slides.notes: If the left side of and is False, Python never runs the right side, so the comparison with None never happens. is_classic needs exactly this shape.

slides.title: Your task, step by step

steps.text: `is_classic(self)`: a year that isn't `None` and is `< 1950`

slides.notes: Everything goes inside class Book(models.Model):, lined up with the title line that's already there. When you're done, try Book.objects.create(title="Emma", author="Jane Austen") in the Console and print it.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: A `CharField` without `max_length`: Django refuses to load the model
Only `null=True` or only `blank=True`: test 2 needs both
`ordering = "title"` (text) instead of a list, or outside `class Meta:`
`__str__` that prints instead of returning, or `<= 1950` instead of `< 1950`

slides.title: Where you'll use this
slides.text: A library app needs to store books, members and loans. Each one is a model, and every screen and API endpoint reads from them.
bullets: After changing a model, run `python manage.py makemigrations`, then `migrate`
The admin, forms and serializers all read their rules from your fields
A good `__str__` turns `Book object (1)` into `Dune by Frank Herbert` in the admin

slides.title: Check yourself
questions: What is the difference between `null=True` and `blank=True`?
Where does `ordering` go, and why does it need square brackets?
Why check `is not None` before comparing a year with 1950?
